traveler: San Te (San-De, 三德), born Liu Yude of Huiyang
title: Three Virtues: the Merchant's Son, the Buckets, and the Thirty-Sixth Chamber
years: c.1718-c.1742 (legendary); first named in a datable text, 1893
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Huiyang, birth in the tea country
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and a calculated one. The postwar novel makes him sixteen in the closing years of the Yongzheng reign, which back-figures to a birth about 1718-1719; no source states a year. No ordination register, genealogy, gazetteer, or household record naming a Liu Yude of Huiyang has been located. District-level coordinates only; no natal site is named anywhere.
stops.campa: In the tea country east of Guangzhou a son is born to a Huiyang family, and they name him Liu Yude. The district keeps no record of the house or the year. What the story keeps is the arm: before he is grown, men who have seen him lift say his arms carry four hundred jin, a figure repeated the way a village repeats a price. His father trades tea and paper ninety miles west in the provincial capital, and keeps a shop there among the Banner households. When the boy is old enough to weigh and count, he is sent down the road to stand behind the counter.
suggested_refs: Huiyang district, Guangdong, given as the family's native place in the 1947-48 novel
sources: I Am a Mountain Man (Chen Jing), Sande heshang san tan Xichan si, ch. 1, qimao.com edition

stops.name: Guangzhou, the tea and paper shop at Shuangmendi
stops.date_confidence: Story time, Yongzheng era; the novel gives no year. Coordinates place the old Hui'ai Street and Shuangmendi quarter approximately within present Yuexiu District. No merchant register, tax roll, or shop sign locates the family's premises.
stops.campa: At Shuangmendi, near Hui'ai Street, the Liu family sells tea and paper in a quarter where Banner households live a few doors from Cantonese shopkeepers. The boy stands behind the counter and weighs leaf into paper. He is large, the neighborhood knows what he can lift, and the two things together make him the kind of youth that trouble finds without having to look for him. Nobody in the garrison that walks this street every day has yet had any reason to learn his name. He weighs out leaf, wraps it, takes the coin, and does it again.
suggested_refs: The Shuangmendi and Hui'ai Street quarter of old Guangzhou, mixed Banner and Cantonese housing
sources: I Am a Mountain Man, Sande heshang san tan Xichan si, ch. 1, qimao.com edition

stops.name: Guangzhou, the fight with Bai Feilong
stops.date_confidence: Story time, Yongzheng era; date assigned only to order the sequence, since the novel places the killings in the reign's final years and gives no month. Literary tradition throughout, with no corresponding Qing judicial record.
stops.campa: Bai Feilong, a martial artist of the Banner garrison, comes into the quarter with his men, and the quarrel that starts in the shop finishes in the street. Liu Yude takes hold of a shopkeeper who has got between them and swings the man's body as a weapon; the shopkeeper dies of it. The novel does not soften the detail and does not apologize for it. An hour earlier the strength was a thing the neighborhood boasted about. The dead man had come out to stop the fight. Liu Yude is sixteen years old.
suggested_refs: The Banner garrison quarter of Guangzhou under Yongzheng
sources: I Am a Mountain Man, Sande heshang san tan Xichan si, ch. 2, qimao.com edition

stops.name: Guangzhou, the chair that kills Shang Hu
stops.date_confidence: Story time, late Yongzheng; month assigned for sequence only. No Qing criminal file, Banner casualty record, or wanted notice corresponding to the death of a deputy commander named Shang Hu at Guangzhou has been located by any research consulted.
stops.campa: The fight the quarter has been expecting arrives, and Shang Hu, deputy commander of the Yellow Banner, comes to settle it in person. Liu Yude kills him with a chair. A Banner officer is not a shopkeeper; the death is a capital matter, and the yamen opens a homicide file the same day, in the name Liu Yude, which he will never again be able to put on anything. By evening the shop is shut and the family is exposed. The son who was to inherit it is walking east, out of the provincial capital, toward the country he was born in.
suggested_refs: Qing law on the killing of a Banner officer by a Han commoner
sources: I Am a Mountain Man, Sande heshang san tan Xichan si, ch. 3, qimao.com edition

stops.name: Huiyang, the fugitive comes home briefly
stops.date_confidence: Story time; the novel gives an order of events, not dates. Reconstruction throughout.
stops.campa: He runs first to the district that bore him, because it is the only ground he knows that is not Guangzhou. Huiyang shelters him briefly and cannot shelter him long: a Banner homicide travels faster than the man who committed it, and every headman in the prefecture has heard the charge before the month is out. He moves again, northeast this time, out of Guangdong altogether, toward the Fujian tea hills where his father once had correspondents. The road he takes is the ordinary overland road of the tea trade. He walks it in the summer of that year, carrying nothing to sell.
suggested_refs: The overland tea route from eastern Guangdong into southern Fujian
sources: I Am a Mountain Man, Sande heshang san tan Xichan si, ch. 3, qimao.com edition

stops.name: Zhangzhou, three months in Lin Boping's house
stops.date_confidence: Story time; the novel specifies about three months of shelter and five hundred taels but no calendar date. City-center coordinates only, since no residence or plantation is named.
stops.campa: In Zhangzhou he finds Lin Boping, a tea grower who did business with his father and means to pay the dead man's account to the son. Lin hides him about three months, feeding him out of the household and telling the neighbors nothing. When it becomes plain that the fugitive cannot stay, Lin gives him five hundred taels, which is not travel money but the price of a life begun over somewhere else. It is the last thing anybody who knew his father ever does for him. Whether Lin was ever questioned about those three months, the novel does not say.
suggested_refs: The Zhangzhou tea trade and its Guangdong correspondents in the eighteenth century
sources: I Am a Mountain Man, Sande heshang san tan Xichan si, ch. 3, qimao.com edition

stops.name: Zhangzhou, the hundred-tael bounty and the monk Yuankong
stops.date_confidence: Story time; sequence attested inside the novel, date assigned to order the segment. The teacher Lin Tiegui, by whom Yuankong recognizes him, appears only in this literary tradition.
stops.campa: A hundred taels are posted for him in Zhangzhou, and a hundred taels in these hills will buy an informer before noon. He leaves the tea grower's house at once. On the road he meets a monk called Yuankong, who hears the whole account out and catches in it the name of the teacher Lin Tiegui, and so understands what is standing in front of him: not a murderer with a bounty on his head but a fighter with nowhere to put the fighting. Yuankong turns him north toward the monastery in the Jiulian hills and walks with him.
suggested_refs: The monk Yuankong, the recruiter figure of the postwar Shaolin cycle
sources: I Am a Mountain Man, Sande heshang san tan Xichan si, ch. 3, qimao.com edition

segments.name: Three Years at the Southern Monastery

stops.name: Fujian Shaolin, Zhi Shan takes him on trial
stops.date_confidence: Story time. The site is one of three competing archaeological candidates for the legendary Southern Shaolin: the Linquan Yuan ruin at Linshan village, Xitianwei town, Putian, excavated 1987 and announced 25 April 1992. Fuqing (excavated 4 June 1993) and Quanzhou's Dongchan Temple are the rivals. None is confirmed as San Te's monastery, and coordinates approximate the Jiulian hills west of Xitianwei rather than a landmark.
stops.campa: The monastery in the Jiulian hills takes fugitives, but not on their own terms. Zhi Shan hears the whole account, the Banner officer and the chair and the bounty, and accepts Liu Yude on trial, which means no ordination, no instruction, and no promise. He is set to whatever the kitchen and the woodlot need. The strength that killed two men in Guangzhou is put to carrying. Nobody in the compound asks him to show what he can do, that first day or for a long time after it.
suggested_refs: The Linquan Yuan excavation at Linshan village, Xitianwei, Putian, one of three claimed Southern Shaolin sites
sources: I Am a Mountain Man, Sande heshang san tan Xichan si, ch. 3, qimao.com edition
Chinese Wikipedia, 南少林寺 and 西天尾鎮

stops.name: Fujian Shaolin, the first year of labor
stops.date_confidence: Story time; the three-year probation is structured by year in the novel, and these dates order that structure rather than record events.
stops.campa: The first year is sweeping, hauling, and the kitchen. He is not taught a form. He watches the ordained monks train in the courtyard and is not invited in, and when he asks he is given more work. This is the standard shape of the southern novice ordeal as the story tells it, and the story insists on the tedium. Zhi Shan watches the whole year and says nothing about what he is watching for. A young man with four hundred jin in his arms spends twelve months moving other people's firewood.
suggested_refs: The novice probation as narrated in the postwar Cantonese Shaolin cycle
sources: I Am a Mountain Man, Sande heshang san tan Xichan si, ch. 3, qimao.com edition

stops.name: Songshan, Henan: the emperor pays to rebuild Shaolin
stops.date_confidence: The 1641 sack of the Henan monastery by Li Zicheng's forces and the court-financed Yongzheng reconstruction of 1735 are attested (Meir Shahar, The Shaolin Monastery, 2008; Wikipedia, Shaolin Monastery). No source places San Te at Songshan, and this is not a visit: it records the documented institution against which the Southern Shaolin legend is measured, pinned at the monastery and dated to the reconstruction so that it sits in story sequence. Popular retellings that collapse San Te's Fujian training into Songshan are conflating two separate traditions.
stops.campa: Fifteen hundred miles north, on Mount Song in Henan, the Yongzheng emperor's treasury pays for the rebuilding of the Shaolin Monastery: the gate, the Thousand Buddha's Hall, the fabric of a house that Li Zicheng's men wrecked in 1641, four years before there was a Qing dynasty to blame for anything. The same court the southern legend says burned Shaolin is at this moment paying to repair it. In Fujian, on the same calendar, the novice is carrying water up a hill and has never heard of Henan.
suggested_refs: Meir Shahar, The Shaolin Monastery: History, Religion, and the Chinese Martial Arts (University of Hawai'i Press, 2008)
sources: Meir Shahar, The Shaolin Monastery (2008)
Wikipedia, Shaolin Monastery, on the 1641 sack and the 1735 reconstruction

stops.name: Fujian Shaolin, the second year: firewood and water
stops.date_confidence: Story time; the quantities are the novel's own and are given without a calendar.
stops.campa: In the second year the load is named and counted: three hundred jin of firewood carried in, fifty loads of water carried up, every day, and the counting is the point. Nobody corrects his stance, because nobody has shown him a stance. He is being built rather than taught. The water comes from a stream below the compound and the path back is uphill the whole way. The novel spends more words on the buckets than on any fight in it, and readers in 1947, taking the story a column at a time in a Guangzhou newspaper, took the buckets as the moral.
suggested_refs: The daily quotas of the second probationary year: three hundred jin of firewood, fifty loads of water
sources: I Am a Mountain Man, Sande heshang san tan Xichan si, ch. 3, qimao.com edition

stops.name: Fujian Shaolin, the third year: the tree
stops.date_confidence: Story time. Tree-striking as a training ordeal is a convention of the postwar cycle; it appears in no earlier text and in no dated martial manual.
stops.campa: In the third year Zhi Shan puts him in front of a tree and tells him to strike it. He strikes it that day and the next and through the season, and the tree does not fall. What changes is the hand. When the trunk finally goes over, the monastery has its answer about him and so does he: the strength he brought up the mountain, which killed a shopkeeper and a Banner officer without a scrap of discipline in it, has been turned into something that can be aimed. He is admitted to the test.
suggested_refs: Tree-striking, the third-year ordeal of the Southern Shaolin novitiate as narrated in 1947
sources: I Am a Mountain Man, Sande heshang san tan Xichan si, ch. 3, qimao.com edition

stops.name: Fujian Shaolin, the tonsure and the name Three Virtues
stops.date_confidence: Story time. The name-bestowal verse is a literary etymology found only in the 1947-48 novel and in no earlier source; the 1893 text simply calls him San Te with no account of where the name came from.
stops.campa: He passes the admission alongside Hong Xiguan and Tong Qianjin, two novices whose names will be bound to his for the next two centuries of retelling, and his head is shaved. Liu Yude of Huiyang, who has a homicide file open in Guangzhou under exactly that name, stops being called it from this morning. Zhi Shan gives him the verse with the new name inside it: the boundless Buddha-dharma aids the completion of my work; one spark of numinous light, Three Virtues shall be his name. San De.
suggested_refs: The tonsure verse of Zhi Shan, source of the monastic name 三德
sources: I Am a Mountain Man, Sande heshang san tan Xichan si, ch. 3, qimao.com edition

stops.name: Fujian Shaolin, sent down to Guangzhou
stops.date_confidence: Story time, Qianlong era; the dispatch is summarized in the later chapters of the 1947-48 novel and the year is assigned only to bridge the two settings. Not independently re-fetched from the qimao text in this pass.
stops.campa: Word comes up the mountain that the monks of Xichan Temple in Guangzhou have let their discipline go: the vinaya loose, the gate open to the wrong company, the house no longer a house of practice. Zhi Shan sends San Te down with Tong Qianjin to put it right. It is an unremarkable errand of monastic administration, and it sends him back into the one city in the empire where his civil name sits on a warrant. Whether Zhi Shan has thought about that, or whether San Te raises it before he goes, the novel never says.
suggested_refs: The Fujian-to-Guangzhou dispatch, hinge between the two halves of the San Te legend
sources: I Am a Mountain Man, Sande heshang san tan Xichan si, later chapters, per dossier summary

segments.name: Xichan Temple in the Western Quarter

stops.name: Guangzhou, Xichan Temple: the house on the turtle's back
stops.date_confidence: Story time, Qianlong era. The temple is real: founded late Tang or early Five Dynasties on a turtle-shaped hill called Guigang, known also as Guifeng and Lingfeng, renovated in the Taiping Xingguo years of the Northern Song (976-984). Coordinates are those of Guangzhou No. 4 Middle School, which stands on the former site, and correct the dossier's earlier figures. This is the Guangzhou Xichan, not the surviving Fuzhou temple of the same name with which English sources routinely confuse it.
stops.campa: Xichan stands in the western quarter of Guangzhou, on a low hill the locals call the turtle's back, and it is old: Guifeng, Lingfeng, a house of the late Tang rebuilt under the Song. San Te comes in as a disciplinarian sent from Fujian and stays as its most famous resident. What he finds inside is not indiscipline so much as a network. Boxers pass through, sleep, eat, and move on, and the gate is understood across the province as a gate that opens for fighters.
suggested_refs: Xichan Temple, Xiguan, Guangzhou (Guifeng or Lingfeng), on the site of the present Guangzhou No. 4 Middle School
sources: Sohu local history of Xichan Temple, Guangzhou (sohu.com/a/683168220_121124386)
Chinese Wikipedia, 西禪寺 (消歧義) and 廣州市第四中學

stops.name: Guangzhou, Xichan Temple: Hu Huiqian hangs the lantern
stops.date_confidence: Attested in the 1893 novel, ch. 14, fetched directly from Chinese Wikisource: the placard 新會胡惠乾專打機房 and the count 共計打死十三人. Story time only; no Guangzhou weaving-guild dispute of the Qianlong era matching this account has been located in any judicial or gazetteer record. Note a live contradiction in the research pool: the quotation below styles San Te as 西禪寺住持, resident abbot, while a direct verification pass reports that ch. 14 treats 住持 as a separate role and calls him only 三德和尚. Not resolved here.
stops.campa: Hu Huiqian of Xinhui comes to the gate with nothing and is taken in and fed like a brother. Then he hangs a lantern in front of the temple announcing that he will fight the weaving workshops of the city, and he does, and thirteen men from the workshops are dead when it is over. The text counts them out: thirteen killed in all. San Te and Hong Xiguan are the steady ones in the house, and the narrator says so while the bodies are still being carried out of the workshop yard.
stops.quote: 西禪寺住持三德和尚及洪熙官乃是老誠之輩，再三勸胡惠乾不可過於滋事
stops.quote_source: Anonymous, Shengchao dingsheng wannianqing, ch. 14, Chinese Wikisource
suggested_refs: The weaving workshops (機房) of Qianlong-era Guangzhou and their guild feuds
sources: Shengchao dingsheng wannianqing, ch. 14, zh.wikisource.org, fetched directly

stops.name: Guangzhou, Xichan Temple: knowing when to stop
stops.date_confidence: The counsel and both quotations are attested in ch. 14, fetched directly, including 凡事知足不辱. A further claim carried by two lenses of the research pool, that San Te and Hong Xiguan were detained by the magistrate and released pending inquiry, was not found on a direct reading of ch. 16 and is not narrated here; see the report.
stops.campa: He puts it to Hu directly. Making trouble here implicates every brother in the house; a monk's reputation will not survive it; and the last killings failed to hang him only because the magistrate chose to look carefully. In all things, he tells him, knowing when to stop keeps a man from disgrace. Hu listens and does nothing. San Te writes to Hu's own first teacher as well, asking him to call his student off, and the letter changes nothing either. The temple goes on feeding him.
stops.quote: 你在這裡生事，連累為兄弟的，出家人聲名不好聽，前日打死眾人，若非縣主明鑒，你性命難逃
stops.quote_source: Anonymous, Shengchao dingsheng wannianqing, ch. 14, Chinese Wikisource
suggested_refs: 凡事知足不辱, San Te's counsel to Hu Huiqian, ch. 14
sources: Shengchao dingsheng wannianqing, ch. 14, zh.wikisource.org, fetched directly

stops.name: Guangzhou, Xichan Temple: Lei Dapeng demands the letters
stops.date_confidence: Attested in the 1893 novel, ch. 16, fetched directly; the chapter was unlocated in the dossier and is confirmed here. Story time only. Note that ch. 16 styles him 三德禪師, Chan master, not 住持.
stops.campa: Lei Dapeng comes to Xichan looking for men who are not there. San Te tells him the truth, that the brothers went home a month ago to visit their families, and Lei answers with a demand and a threat: write now, call them all back to meet me, this is no business of yours as a monk, and if you do not write, do not blame me for what I do to your monks. The record is exact about the direction of the pressure: San Te is not convening a network of fighters, he is being made to hold a pen under a threat to every monk in the house. He writes the letters.
stops.quote: 你速寫信，叫各人前來會我，不干你出家人之事，若不寫信，莫怪我得罪你各僧人。
stops.quote_source: Anonymous, Shengchao dingsheng wannianqing, ch. 16, Chinese Wikisource
suggested_refs: Chapter 16, 雷大鵬別師下山　胡惠乾送兒入寺
sources: Shengchao dingsheng wannianqing, ch. 16, zh.wikisource.org, fetched directly

stops.name: Guangzhou, Guangxiao Temple: the brothers assemble
stops.date_confidence: Attested in ch. 16, fetched directly. Coordinates are those of Guangxiao Temple in Yuexiu District, Guangzhou, a real and surviving monastery; the gathering itself is literary.
stops.campa: The letters go out fast. San Te writes them with Hong Xiguan and Tong Qianjin, urgent notice to every brother of the school. The men who read them do not come to Xichan; they assemble instead at Guangxiao Temple in the heart of the provincial city, while Hu Huiqian goes back alone to the house in the western quarter. From here the story stops being a quarrel between a boxer and a weaving guild and becomes something the provincial government has to hold an opinion about. Guangxiao is the oldest monastery in the city, and it is standing there yet.
stops.quote: 三德和尚急忙與洪熙官、童千斤等飛信通知各人，各師兄弟聞言，即到省城光孝寺聚集。
stops.quote_source: Anonymous, Shengchao dingsheng wannianqing, ch. 16, Chinese Wikisource
suggested_refs: Guangxiao Temple (光孝寺), Guangzhou, muster point of the Shaolin brothers in ch. 16
sources: Shengchao dingsheng wannianqing, ch. 16, zh.wikisource.org, fetched directly

segments.name: A Thousand Guards and a Thousand Archers

stops.name: Guangzhou, the governor's order
stops.date_confidence: Attested in the 1893 novel, ch. 61, as literary narrative. No Qing military report, provincial memorial, or garrison order corresponding to an operation against a Guangzhou temple has been located; the figures are the novel's. Coordinates place the provincial governor's seat approximately in Yuexiu, since no yamen address is given in the text.
stops.campa: Zeng Bizhong, governor of Guangdong, gives the order from his yamen in the eastern part of the city. The middle army of his own standard and the commanding officers of three battalions are to take a thousand guards and a thousand archers, to carry strong bows and hard crossbows, and to go quietly at the third watch tonight and surround Xichan Temple. The court has already sent Gao Jinzhong south to take San Te and Hu Huiqian. Two thousand men are being moved against a temple in order to arrest two.
stops.quote: 命令本標中軍及三營統兵官，命他們帶領親兵一千，弓箭手一千，多備強弓硬弩，於今夜三更暗暗前往，將西禪寺圍住
stops.quote_source: Anonymous, Shengchao dingsheng wannianqing, ch. 61, Chinese Wikisource
suggested_refs: Chapter 61 of the 1893 novel, the order to surround Xichan Temple
sources: Shengchao dingsheng wannianqing, ch. 61, per the research pool's chapter citation

stops.name: Guangzhou, Xichan Temple: the ring closes at the third watch
stops.date_confidence: Attested in the 1893 novel, ch. 62. Story time; no date is given in the text and none is recoverable from any external record.
stops.campa: San Te does the arithmetic out loud for Hu Huiqian before anything starts. Two fists cannot beat four hands. Under a heavy reward there is always a brave man, and under a general anger there will always be a fight to the death. If the government troops come they will not come as one or two hundred; there will be a thousand eight hundred at the least, and no amount of skill answers that. He wants them out of the city tonight, north to Fujian, to put the whole thing in front of Zhi Shan and let the old man decide what is to be done about it.
stops.quote: 雙拳難敵四手。又道：『重賞之下，必有勇夫。眾怒之下，必然死戰。』若果是官兵前來，必非一二百人，至少也有一千八百，任憑你我再有本領，豈能敵得他們如此之多？...還是及早逃走，去往福建少林寺暫避風波，隨後再看光景，或請至善禪師設法。
stops.quote_source: Anonymous, Shengchao dingsheng wannianqing, ch. 62, Chinese Wikisource
suggested_refs: Chapter 62, San Te's counsel of flight to Fujian
sources: Shengchao dingsheng wannianqing, ch. 62, per the research pool's chapter citation

stops.name: Guangzhou, Xichan Temple: the head thrown across the courtyard
stops.date_confidence: Attested verbatim in ch. 63, fetched directly. A detail carried in the dossier, that San Te accidentally splits the head with his own blade before learning Hu is dead, is not in the text and has been dropped: the text says only that the head struck him.
stops.campa: Gao Jinzhong takes Hu Huiqian's head off in the courtyard and throws it. It strikes San Te on the head, which the narrator concedes is the kind of coincidence only a book allows. A thrown knife has already opened San Te's right hand. He does not yet know that the object which has just hit him is the man he warned, wrote letters for, and fed at this gate. Around him the courtyard is full of soldiers who have been told they are putting down criminal monks. The lanterns are still lit.
stops.quote: 將胡惠乾的首級擲了出去，無巧不成書，偏巧那頭剛剛打在三德和尚頭上。
stops.quote_source: Anonymous, Shengchao dingsheng wannianqing, ch. 63, Chinese Wikisource
suggested_refs: Chapter 63, the death of Hu Huiqian
sources: Shengchao dingsheng wannianqing, ch. 63, zh.wikisource.org, fetched directly

stops.name: Guangzhou, Xichan Temple: the death of San Te
stops.date_confidence: Attested verbatim in ch. 63, fetched directly, including 在他的左膊之上 and 將三德砍為肉餅. This is the earliest datable death narrative of the character, published 1893, framed by a narrator loyal to the Qing and hostile to him. No burial, date, successor, or relic is given in the chapter or anywhere else.
stops.campa: He says it is bad, his hand loosens, and the sword rings on the flagstones. Fang De comes in on that opening and puts a heavy cut into his left shoulder. He cries out once and goes down, and the whole party closes over him with blades and spears until, in the words of the earliest account there is, they hack San Te into a meat patty. The crowd is described as pleased. There is no funeral in the chapter, no grave, no successor named, and no monk of Xichan is mentioned again.
stops.quote: 三德說聲不好，手一鬆，只聽叮噹一聲，手中刀已拋落在地。接著方德就在這個當兒，又砍進一刀，在他的左膊之上用勁一下。三德哇呀一聲，登時跌倒在地，當由眾夥伴一齊上來，刀槍齊施，將三德砍為肉餅。
stops.quote_source: Anonymous, Shengchao dingsheng wannianqing, ch. 63, Chinese Wikisource
suggested_refs: Chapter 63, the earliest datable death narrative of San Te
sources: Shengchao dingsheng wannianqing, ch. 63, zh.wikisource.org, fetched directly

stops.name: Guangzhou, Xichan Temple becomes a police station
stops.date_confidence: Attested and quoted verbatim in a Sohu local-history article: 清光緒三十三年（1907），當時幽靜佛寺竟被用來做了政府機關，巡警西關第二分局. Month unknown, defaulted to January. That article names no connection whatever to San Te.
stops.campa: The temple outlives the story by a century and a half and then stops being a temple. In the thirty-third year of Guangxu the provincial government takes the quiet Buddhist house in the western quarter and installs the Second Sub-Bureau of the Xiguan police in it. Monks are not mentioned in the transfer. The buildings the novel filled with two thousand soldiers are filled instead with constables, files, and a duty desk. The hill underneath keeps the name the locals gave it.
suggested_refs: The Second Sub-Bureau of the Xiguan police, installed in Xichan Temple, 1907
sources: Sohu local history of Xichan Temple, Guangzhou (sohu.com/a/683168220_121124386)

stops.name: Guangzhou, the temple sold at auction
stops.date_confidence: Attested in the Sohu local history: the municipal government auctioned the site in 1924 to raise funds for the Northern Expedition, at a reserve of 150 yuan, and it was demolished. Month unknown, defaulted to January. This account is flatly contradicted by the Chinese Wikipedia disambiguation page for 西禪寺, which says the Guangzhou temple was destroyed after the Southern Han gave way to the Song, in the tenth century. The two cannot both be right; neither is preferred here.
stops.campa: In 1924 the municipal government puts the ground up for auction to raise money for the Northern Expedition, at a reserve price of one hundred and fifty yuan. It sells. The buildings come down. Whatever inscriptions the house held, whatever abbatial tablets, whatever roll of resident monks ran back to the Song, go down with them, and nobody at the sale is recorded as having looked. Who bought the ground, and what the hundred and fifty yuan finally paid for, the account does not say.
suggested_refs: The 1924 municipal auction of the Xichan Temple site, reserve price 150 yuan

stops.name: Guangzhou, a school on the old ground
stops.date_confidence: The Sohu article states verbatim that in 1933 the former ground of Xichan Temple was built as Guangzhou Municipal No. 51 Primary School, not as the middle school the dossier named. Guangzhou No. 4 Middle School, which occupies the address today, dates its own founding to 1917 on the site of the Buddhist temple Xichan, which is nine years before the demolition the Sohu article describes. The conflict is recorded, not adjudicated. Month unknown, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: Nine years after the demolition a school goes up on the site: Guangzhou Municipal No. 51 Primary School, built on the old ground of Xichan Temple. Children are taught where the courtyard was. The address today is 1 Luodi Street, off Kangwang North Road in Liwan District, and what stands there is Guangzhou No. 4 Middle School, an institution whose own account has it founded in 1917 on the site of the famous Buddhist temple Xichan. That is nine years before the temple came down.

stops.name: Shanghai, the Five Colors Company prints the first parts
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to year and publisher in the Chinese Wikipedia entry for 聖朝鼎盛萬年青; month unknown, defaulted to January. General Shanghai coordinates only, no press address located. This is the earliest securely datable appearance of the name San Te in any document.
stops.campa: In Shanghai a lithographic press called the Five Colors Company begins issuing an anonymous Cantonese novel in parts: Shengchao dingsheng wannianqing, seventy-six chapters of the Qianlong emperor touring the south and the boxer-monks who make trouble in his path. The politics belong to the emperor. Shaolin is the criminal party, and San Te dies a rebel's death in chapter sixty-three at the hands of soldiers the book approves of. This is the first time in any datable document that anybody is called San Te.
suggested_refs: Shengchao dingsheng wannianqing (聖朝鼎盛萬年青), anonymous, 76 chapters

stops.name: Shanghai, parts three and four from a second house
stops.date_confidence: Attested verbatim: 光緒二十二年（1896年），上海書局續印三、四集. This corrects the dossier, which attributed the continuation to the Five Colors Company. Month unknown, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: Parts three and four follow from a different house, the Shanghai Book Company, in the twenty-second year of Guangxu. The novel is doing what serial fiction does: changing publishers, adding continuations, losing whatever authorial control it had at the start. The anonymity is not modesty; a book that turns named martial brotherhoods into criminals is a book with a reason to keep its author off the cover. By now the Guangzhou chapters circulate in the south on their own, detached from the imperial tour they were written to frame. Nobody signs it, in this printing or in any later one.
suggested_refs: 上海書局 (Shanghai Book Company), publisher of the 1896 continuation
sources: Chinese Wikipedia, 聖朝鼎盛萬年青, publication-history section, fetched directly

stops.name: Shanghai, the pocket edition in twelve fascicles
stops.date_confidence: Attested verbatim: 光緒三十年（1904年），上海書局石印巾箱本全十二冊. The variant titles are confirmed verbatim in the same entry. Month unknown, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: In the thirtieth year of Guangxu the Shanghai Book Company brings out a lithographed pocket edition, twelve fascicles, small enough to carry in a sleeve. A reader who buys it for the southern tour gets the monk's death in it whether he wants it or not. From here the book travels under whatever title a printer prefers: Wannianqing, Wannianqing qicai xinzhuan, Qianlong xunxing Jiangnan ji, an illustrated Qianlong you Jiangnan, Qianlong xia Jiangnan. The emperor's name migrates into every one of them, and San Te's into none.
suggested_refs: The 1904 巾箱本 lithograph in twelve fascicles, and the novel's variant titles
sources: Chinese Wikipedia, 聖朝鼎盛萬年青, fetched directly

stops.name: Shanghai, the dictionary fixes the name
stops.date_confidence: The entry 三德 in Ding Fubao's Foxue da cidian is attested and was fetched directly from Chinese Wikisource. The 1922 compilation date is carried from the dossier and was not independently verified. The entry gives four distinct senses; the Nirvana triad is 法身德, 般若德, 解脫德, while 智德 and 斷德 belong to a separate triad with 恩德 and are not alternate labels for the first two, as the dossier had it. No sense resembling harmony appears anywhere in the entry.
stops.campa: Ding Fubao assembles his Great Dictionary of Buddhist Studies, and under the head 三德 he sets out what the two characters meant long before any novelist borrowed them. The Nirvana Sutra's three virtues of great nirvana: the virtue of the dharma-body, the virtue of prajna, the virtue of liberation, arranged, the entry says, like the three dots of the letter i. Three further senses follow, among them wisdom, severance, and grace. Nowhere in the entry is there a sense that could be rendered as harmony.
stops.quote: 涅槃經所說大涅槃所具之三德：一、法身德，為佛之本體，以常住不滅之法性為身者。

stops.name: Guangzhou, the Guangdong Shangbao begins the serial
stops.date_confidence: The serialization in Guangdong Shangbao from July 1947 to June 1948 is carried from Chen Longting (Taiwan Historica 68.3, 2017) and Chen Dawei (Wen yu Zhe 42, 2023) as cited in the dossier; the titles and venues of both articles were verified, their contents were not re-fetched. The Chinese Wikipedia entry for the author supports none of this bibliographic scaffolding: it names him 陳勁, also 陳魯勁, born 1916, died 25 August 1974, and gives no newspaper, publisher, or 1947-48 date. Day defaulted to the first.
stops.campa: In a Guangzhou newspaper, the Guangdong Shangbao, a writer signing himself I Am a Mountain Man begins the serial that gives San Te a life. His name is Chen Jing. Across eleven months he invents everything the 1893 book never had: the civil name Liu Yude, Huiyang, the tea and paper shop, the Banner officer, the flight to Zhangzhou, the three years of buckets, the tonsure verse. He also turns the politics inside out. The monk the imperial novel executed as a criminal becomes the hero, and the dynasty becomes the enemy.
suggested_refs: 我是山人 (Chen Jing, 陳勁, 1916-1974), Sande heshang san tan Xichan si

stops.name: Hong Kong, the book in five volumes
stops.date_confidence: Disputed and left disputed. A collector's examination of copyright pages argues for a five-volume Xiongming Publishing House first edition, volume 1 about May 1948 and volume 5 dated 18 October 1948; Chen Longting instead cites a Hong Kong Dazhong Book Company edition of 1947. The preface date is given as March 1948 by one profile. The editions cannot be reconciled from the accessible evidence. General Hong Kong coordinates only; no publisher address located.
stops.campa: The serial closes and the book follows, five volumes, the first out around May and the fifth dated the eighteenth of October. The country it is written for has just come out of eight years of Japanese occupation, and San Te, dead two centuries inside a story and never once alive outside one, is put to work in it as evidence that the Chinese body was always strong. A preface states the purpose without ornament: to popularize Chinese martial arts, and to wash away the shame of the sick man of East Asia.

stops.name: Ngau Chi Wan, Golden Harvest: The Iron-Fisted Monk
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the Hong Kong Film Archive programme page gives the film, cast, and 93-minute colour 35mm Cantonese specification, and the 25 August 1977 release date is confirmed. The studio is corrected here: Golden Harvest bought the former Cathay lot on King Tung Street in Ngau Chi Wan, not Diamond Hill, and operated it from 1970 to 1998; the site is now Charm Peak Towers.
stops.campa: On King Tung Street in Ngau Chi Wan, in a lot Golden Harvest bought from Cathay, Sammo Hung directs his first film and puts San Te at the center of it. Chan Sing plays the monk as a Shaolin-trained teacher against the Qing; Hung plays Rice-Pounding Six, the layman he trains. It is the first time the monk exists as a body in motion rather than a column of characters, and the body doing most of the moving belongs to the director. Ninety-three minutes, colour, 35mm, Cantonese, released on the twenty-fifth of August.

stops.name: Tai Po Tsai, Shaw Movietown: The 36th Chamber of Shaolin
stops.date_confidence: The 2 February 1978 Hong Kong premiere is confirmed; the Hong Kong Film Archive dates the production itself to 1977 and gives 111 minutes, against the 115 minutes carried by English Wikipedia. stops.campa: At Shaw Movietown in Tai Po Tsai, out on the Clear Water Bay peninsula, Lau Kar-leung films the version that swallows all the others. Gordon Liu is Liu Yude, then San Te. Ni Kuang writes it. The thirty-five chambers of training, each a room holding one lesson, and the thirty-sixth that San Te founds so laypeople may learn, are invented here and appear in no earlier text at all. Fifteen years later a group of rappers on Staten Island takes its debut album's title and its whole organizing metaphor out of those rooms.

stops.name: Tai Po Tsai, Shaw Movietown: somebody pretends to be him
stops.date_confidence: Attested: released 24 August 1980, directed by Lau Kar-leung, a Shaw Brothers production, with Lee King-chue credited as Abbot San Te and Gordon Liu as the impersonator, romanized Chu Jen-chieh in English listings. This corrects the dossier, which had anchored the film to the Golden Harvest lot.
stops.campa: Lau Kar-leung brings Gordon Liu back to Shaw Movietown for the sequel and does not let him play the monk. Liu plays a scaffolding worker who impersonates San Te to bluff his way through a labor dispute. Two years after the film that made him, the character is settled enough in the audience that a whole comedy can be built out of somebody pretending to be him. The real San Te is a minor role, credited to Lee King-chue. Released on the twenty-fourth of August.

stops.name: Tai Po Tsai, Shaw Movietown: the abbot and Fang Shiyu
stops.date_confidence: Year attested from standard film-reference records; month and day unknown and defaulted. The specific cast attribution was carried from the dossier's citation of Shaw catalogue material and was not independently re-fetched in this pass.
stops.campa: Lau Kar-leung's third pass, and Gordon Liu is San Te again, no longer the novice who broke a tree but the institution itself: an established master trying to get discipline into Fang Shiyu, who does not want any. Inside seven years of one studio's output the character has travelled from fugitive student to exasperated abbot. The 1893 novel gave the monk exactly one function, to counsel a violent young man who ignores him, and the films have arrived back at that function from the other end.

stops.name: Guangzhou, Xichan Temple: the politics turned over
stops.date_confidence: Chen Longting's article in Taiwan Historica 68.3 is attested as to title, author, venue, and September 2017 date; its contents are summarized from the dossier's claim-map and were not re-fetched. Day defaulted. The stop is pinned at the temple the argument is about, not at the scholar's desk. The puppetry repertoire 再建少林寺 is documented as performed from 1950 in the same study.
stops.campa: Chen Longting publishes in Taiwan Historica the account of what happened to the politics. The 1893 novel is an imperial book in which Shaolin is the criminal party; the postwar Cantonese novels reverse it wholesale, and a monk executed as a rebel by a loyal narrator becomes the rebel hero. Nothing in the plot had to change for it, only who the reader was expected to be. The reversed version is the one that reaches Taiwanese glove puppetry, where the repertoire Rebuilding Shaolin Temple has been performed since 1950.

stops.name: Guangzhou, Xichan Temple: the search of the registers
stops.date_confidence: A negative finding, stated as one. No eighteenth-century ordination register, Xichan inscription or abbatial list, Fujian or Henan monastery roll, Qing memorial, criminal file, wanted notice, military report, execution record, gazetteer entry, family genealogy, merchant record, or dated martial manual naming San Te or Liu Yude has been located by any research consulted. The completeness of the archival search behind that statement could not itself be verified. Dated to Chen Dawei's June 2023 study in Wen yu Zhe 42, pp. 317-344, and pinned at the temple; day defaulted.
stops.campa: No ordination register names him. No inscription from Xichan, no abbatial list, no Fujian or Henan monastery roll, no Qing memorial, no criminal file, no wanted notice, no military report on a temple stormed at Guangzhou, no local gazetteer, no genealogy of a Liu family in Huiyang, no dated martial manual. Chen Dawei traces the whole modern idea of Shaolin back through the postwar Cantonese novelists and finds them standing at the head of it. The earliest datable San Te is a printed page from 1893. There is no grave to visit.
